title: Async cooperative mini-batcher: probe notes and hypotheses
content:
Purpose:
Quick working notes from probes into a new async cooperative mini-batcher prototype (`mini-batcher`) that attempts to collect very small requests into micro-batches inside the Python process

Observations so far (experiment logs):
- Experiment harness: local dev machine (c6i-like CPU), 8 cores, python3.11, pypy not tested. Tokenizer is fastBPE (C extension) exposed via CFFI.
- Baseline: single-request path median p95=8.3ms, p99=14.7ms under synthetic workload (r=200/s).
- Mini-batcher enabled (cooperative async wait 200us window): p95=9.6ms (+15%), p99=22.1ms (+50%) — tail regressed.
- CPU profiles (perf+flamegraphs) show increased time in:
  - Python scheduler overhead (PyEval_EvalFrameEx / interpreter state switches)
  - syscall wait loops inside event loop (short sleeps)
  - tokenizer CFFI boundary calls appearing slightly more often per request due to speculative tokenization attempts

What we measured (snippets):
- microbench harness output (representative):
  requests: 10k, concurrency: 4, batch-window: 200us
  median latency: 6.1ms
  p95 latency: 9.6ms
  p99 latency: 22.1ms
  CPU util: 62% (user), 6% (sys), small I/O waits

- perf top / annotated stack (summary):
  25% PyThreadState_Swap (context switching between green-threads)
  18% PyEval_EvalFrameEx (bytecode evaluation during batching loop)
  12% CFFI_call_fastbpe_tokenize (tokenization time)
  8% epoll_wait and nanosleep (micro-sleep coordination)

Hypotheses (root causes):
1) Cooperative polling window creates bursts of interpreter activity that serialize with tokenizer C calls, increasing contention on the Python thread and amplifying tail latency.
2) Short sleeps (nanosleep/epoll timeouts) used to implement a batching window produce syscall jitter and scheduler wakeups; when combined with many worker coroutines it increases context-switch noise.
3) Tokenizer CFFI re-entrancy: if tokenization holds a GIL-like lock or long C work, other coroutines are starved; our mini-batcher increases frequency of tokenization calls per unit time, worsening head-of-line blocking.
4) Per-request micro-allocation churn in the batching path increases GC pressure and Sporadic GC pauses correlate with p99 spikes in some runs.

Quick experiments to validate hypotheses (what we ran):
- Disable micro-sleep (busy-wait spin for 50us) -> tail improved on local run but CPU doubled; suggests syscalls are a factor.
- Move tokenization to a shared tokenization threadpool (offload via concurrent.futures.ThreadPoolExecutor) -> median unchanged, p99 reduced ~18% in one trial but introduced threadpool queue latencies at high load.
- Increase batch-window to 500us -> p95 improves slightly but p99 sometimes spikes more due to larger grouping when a slow tokenization call stalls the group.
- Run with tracemalloc and smaller heap to trigger more frequent GC; p99 correlates with GC collections in ~30% of bursts.

Open questions / unknowns:
- Does the tokenizer C module release the GIL during heavy work? (need to inspect source or run Python-level GIL contention tools)
- Are we seeing Python-level scheduling (PyThreadState) or OS-level preemption? perf and py-spy show both — need a combined timeline.
- What is the sweet spot for window size vs CPU cost for production fleet? (need param sweep with realistic request distribution)

Suggested next steps (concrete):
1) Add a small trace timeline per request that includes: enqueue_ts, batch_start_ts, tokenizer_enter_ts, tokenizer_exit_ts, send_ts. This will let us attribute tail-causes to tokenizer vs scheduling. (owner: Ben)
2) Run a kernel-timer+py-spy combined capture on a staging node under realistic QPS with 12 cores. Use perf record -g + py-spy to correlate C stacks and Python frames. (owner: Carmen)
3) Instrument tokenizer C extension to assert whether it releases the GIL and emit micro-metrics (tokenize_ms per call) for 48h. (owner: Diego)
4) Prototype a hybrid: small busy-spin for first 50us then fall back to epoll_wait; benchmark CPU vs tail tradeoffs. (owner: Aisha)
5) Try a minimal Rust tokenizer shim that exposes an async-friendly interface (releases the GIL entirely) for a controlled A/B test. Note: this is heavier but will isolate the GIL hypothesis. (owner: roadmap)

Experiment notes / commands used: (for reproducibility)
- harness run: ./tools/mini-batch-harness --qps 200 --concurrency 4 --batch-window-us 200 --duration 300s --payload small
- perf capture: sudo perf record -F 99 -p <pid> -g -- sleep 60; sudo perf script > perf.stacks
- py-spy: sudo py-spy record -o profile.svg --pid <pid> --duration 60
- tok profiler: export TOK_DEBUG=1; ./service --enable-tok-metrics

Low-effort mitigations to try in prod (can be toggled):
- Increase default batch-window slightly (e.g., 200 -> 350us) behind a flag for tiered customers. Trade: slightly higher median but fewer p99 spikes seen in early trials.
- Route requests that are likely short (few tokens predicted) to a separate fast-path bypassing batching. Need heuristic: content-length, header hints.
- Add GC tuning: increase object arena to reduce frequency of small GCs; run with PYTHONMALLOC=malloc or tuned GC thresholds for the process.

Notes to self / rough TODO list:
- Check GH-hr/mini-batcher-PR-512 for recent changes to sleep/backoff code (Ben).
- Add flamegraph of combined C/Python frames to the Confluence page.
- Schedule pairing session with tokenizer team to confirm GIL behavior.

Preliminary conclusion (working):
Mini-batching at microsecond windows is promising for cost but sensitive to interpreter-level scheduling and C-extension behavior. The p99 regressions appear to be a mix of syscall wakeup jitter and tokenization-induced serialization. Resolving this will likely be: 1) ensure tokenization releases the GIL or run it on an independent worker, 2) replace short sleeps with hybrid spin/epoll logic, and 3) add tracing so we can attribute tail spikes to a single component rather than the black-box batching layer.

Signed-off-by: Aisha (quick notes, not final doc)
